title: TakeShape Adventures operations dashboard
category: Ops dashboard, WooCommerce, Keap and Meta
summary: A staff operations dashboard for an adventure travel company: every departure's manifest and check-in, trip pages edited and published back to WordPress, and the Keap and Meta automations that used to live in third-party glue, all running off one Postgres database.

image.alt: The locations workspace: a list of trip locations sorted by what needs attention, and the Freycinet Peninsula record open with its publish checklist and a prompt to publish edits to WordPress.

caseStudy.heading: One place to run the trips, with WordPress, Keap and Meta kept in step behind it.
caseStudy.intro: TakeShape Adventures sells guided hikes and multi-day trips through a WordPress and WooCommerce site, keeps its contacts in Keap and finds new customers through Meta ads. I built the staff dashboard that sits across all of it: departures and check-in, trip content, orders, and the automations between Keap and Meta.

sections.heading: The problem
paragraphs: The bookings happen in WooCommerce, the contacts live in Keap, the leads arrive from Meta ads, and the trip pages are WordPress taxonomy terms with a lot of custom fields. Each of those tools did its own job. None of them could tell a guide at 5:30 in the morning who was booked on today's walk, who had a dietary flag, and who had already arrived.

[One or two lines in the client's words about what running a departure looked like before: printed lists, WP admin, phone calls.] The glue between Keap tags and Meta audiences, and between Meta lead forms and Keap contacts, also needed somewhere it could be watched and fixed when it failed.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: A Next.js dashboard backed by Postgres that mirrors what it needs from each system and writes back where staff need to edit. A small WordPress plugin I wrote serves the endpoints it reads and writes, and pings the dashboard when an order or a trip changes, so a booking shows up in seconds rather than on the next scheduled pass.
steps: Departures and check-in: every upcoming trip with capacity, crew and a manifest per booking party. One tap checks a party in, with crew notes, no-shows and a CSV export for the day.
Locations: the trip pages edited in the dashboard, including highlights, itinerary, packing lists, gallery images and a publish checklist, then published back to the WordPress term.
Client info forms: each location defines the questions guests answer in the member app after booking, with presets, required fields and due dates counted back from departure.
Zaps: Keap tags kept in step with Meta custom audiences, and Meta lead form submissions turned into tagged Keap contacts, with every attempt logged and failures surfaced with their reason.
Orders, contacts, a resource library aimed at locations, trip types or states, and a BullMQ worker that runs the scheduled syncs.

figure.alt: The Meta lead forms to Keap zap: four stat tiles, an amber alert explaining two failures, and a mapping shown as a Meta trigger panel with three lead forms and a Keap action panel with three tags.
figure.caption: Each zap shows its mappings as trigger and action, and every attempt it makes. A rejected field mapping fails on its own and says why, instead of costing the lead.

sections.heading: The hard part
paragraphs: Syncing four systems that each think they are the source of truth. WooCommerce deletes and recreates order line items on every update, so check-ins are keyed on a stable order and item pair rather than the row, and a re-sync never loses who arrived. Syncs can be triggered by a button, the schedule and the WordPress ping at once, so every one takes a Postgres advisory lock per organisation and kind, and a collision is skipped rather than allowed to fight over the same rows.

The edges are where the trust is. Meta lead webhooks must be signed or they are rejected, Keap deliveries are authenticated by a secret in the callback URL because Keap does not sign them, and OAuth callbacks re-derive the organisation from the session so a forged state cannot attach tokens to the wrong account. Client info answers arrive from the member app encrypted with AES-256-GCM and stay encrypted at rest; they are decrypted only inside the request that shows them to a staff member. When stock is not managed in WooCommerce, capacity is shown as unknown rather than guessed.

figure.alt: The Three Capes location on its Client info tab: a Medical and dietary section with a required multiple choice question about dietary requirements, due 14 days before the trip, and its stable field key shown underneath.
figure.caption: The client info builder. A question's key is issued once and never changes, because the member app files every answer under it.

sections.heading: How it went
paragraphs: The first version went in during August 2025 on a starter kit that read the WordPress database directly. In July 2026 I rebuilt it on a stronger base, moved WordPress access behind a REST plugin, and took the chance to fix what the first version got wrong: a PHP serialisation parser that broke on quotes, tags that could leak between organisations, and a capacity number that was invented. [What the team stopped doing once check-in moved into the dashboard.] It runs in production on Coolify, and I'm still adding to it.

asideCta.heading: Running your business across four tools that don't talk?
asideCta.body: Tell me what each one holds and where the work falls through the gaps, and I'll tell you what I'd build.

notes: Rewritten from the code in ~/Projects/tsa-stack/tsadash (v2) and ~/Projects/tsadashboard (v1). Corrections to the old seed: this is not a CRM that replaced a 'generic CRM'. Keap stays as the CRM and the dashboard syncs with it. Bookings come from WooCommerce (pushed by a WordPress mu-plugin), not directly from the mobile app; the member app (tsa-app, Expo + Supabase) only exchanges client info forms and submissions with it. The membership tier claim was dropped (only a members price field is visible here). Code-derived numbers: 41 TSA Prisma models (59 including the SaaS base), 18 org tRPC routers, 244 test cases in 19 files, 12 REST routes in a 2,197-line mu-plugin, 10 BullMQ job types; Liam's commits: 42 in v1 (Aug 2025 to Jul 2026) and 50 in v2 (27 Jul to 9 Sep 2026). Check: (1) the v2 base is a purchased SaaS template (Achromatic licence, Mahmut Jomaa commits) and v1 was a Next 15 starter kit; the copy says 'starter kit' and 'stronger base' without naming them. Decide whether to credit or omit. (2) Production URL is stagingcrm.takeshapeadventures.com.au; screenshots show crm.takeshapeadventures.com.au instead. (3) All names, phone numbers (555 range), emails (example.com), order numbers, trip names, Facebook form names and Keap tag names in the images are fictional; the categories 'Women only' and 'Water' are invented. (4) The CLAUDE.md 'Known gaps' at migration time said no sync had been run against live credentials; later commits (Coolify hosting, Keap phone slots, timezone fixes) indicate it is live, but confirm. (5) Placeholders left: [N hrs] stat, the problem paragraph quote, and what the team stopped doing. No client quote included.
